policy_text:
Claiming a dependent on a 2026 federal return: qualifying child and qualifying relative tests
A taxpayer may claim the person as a dependent only if every rule below is met. Rules about a qualifying child apply only when the person is claimed as a qualifying child, and rules about a qualifying relative only when claimed as a qualifying relative. Rules marked as defaults say what to assume when the return is silent on a point.

R1. The person must be a U.S. citizen, U.S. national, U.S. resident alien, or a resident of Canada or Mexico, unless the taxpayer is a U.S. citizen who legally adopted the person and the person lived with the taxpayer all year.
R2. A qualifying child must be under age 19 at the end of the year.
R3. A qualifying child must be younger than the taxpayer, unless permanently and totally disabled.
R4. If disability is not mentioned, assume the person is not permanently and totally disabled.
R5. The taxpayer must provide more than half of a qualifying relative's total support, unless a signed multiple support agreement (Form 2120) names the taxpayer, who provides more than 10% of the support.
R6. A qualifying child must have lived with the taxpayer for more than half the year (7 months or more).
R7. A qualifying relative may not be the qualifying child of any other taxpayer.
R8. A qualifying relative who is not a listed relative (a cousin is not listed, but in-laws, parents, siblings, nieces and nephews are) must have lived with the taxpayer all year.
case_text: File 8737 documents the tax return preparation for Luis Ortega. Luis Ortega reached age 23 by December 31, 2026. Luis provided 75% of the total financial support for the individual during the year. No other filer is eligible to claim Luis as a dependent on their tax return. The client mentions that the individual assists significantly with household chores. The individual maintained residency in the client's household for 4 months throughout 2026. A prior accident resulted in the individual's permanent and total disability. Luis is older than the individual by a margin of 4 years. Official documentation confirms the individual holds U.S. citizenship. The individual cannot be claimed as a qualifying child by any other taxpayer. The U.S. citizen client completed a legal adoption of the individual. The individual is related to Luis as a cousin. The custodial parent has withheld execution of Form 8332 regarding the exemption release. The individual attained the age of 19 by the conclusion of 2026. Combining wages, taxable interest, and rental receipts prior to deductions, the individual's gross income totals $10,700. The tax professional noted an expedited filing requested to accelerate the anticipated refund. Taxable interest reported by the individual amounted to $500. Employment earnings for the individual reached $9,000 in wages. The individual's parents have not listed them as dependents on any tax filing. The client seeks to claim the individual under the provisions for a qualifying relative. The couple submits a joint filing solely to recover withheld taxes. The individual contributed 0% toward their own living expenses across the tax year. Academic transcripts verify full-time student status spanning at least 5 calendar months in 2026. Attached to the paperwork is a completed Form 2120 multiple support declaration designating Luis. This tax season marks the taxpayer's initial engagement with a professional preparer. The tax preparer has maintained a professional relationship with the family for multiple years. Gross rental income collected from a tenant by the individual prior to expenses was $1,200. The individual maintains marital status and submitted a joint tax return alongside their spouse. Residency outside the primary home during the remaining months did not qualify as a temporary absence.

policy_text:
Claiming a dependent on a 2026 federal return: qualifying child and qualifying relative tests
A taxpayer may claim the person as a dependent only if every rule below is met. Rules about a qualifying child apply only when the person is claimed as a qualifying child, and rules about a qualifying relative only when claimed as a qualifying relative. Rules marked as defaults say what to assume when the return is silent on a point.

R1. A qualifying relative may not be the qualifying child of any other taxpayer.
R2. The taxpayer must provide more than half of a qualifying relative's total support, unless a signed multiple support agreement (Form 2120) names the taxpayer, who provides more than 10% of the support.
R3. A qualifying child must be under age 19 at the end of the year, unless the person was a full-time student for at least 5 months of the year and is under 24.
R4. A qualifying relative who is not a listed relative (a cousin is not listed, but in-laws, parents, siblings, nieces and nephews are) must have lived with the taxpayer all year.
R5. A taxpayer who can be claimed as someone else's dependent may not claim any dependent.
R6. If the return does not say the person is another taxpayer's qualifying child, assume they are not.
R7. A qualifying child must be younger than the taxpayer, unless permanently and totally disabled.
R8. If no multiple support agreement is mentioned, assume there is none.
R9. The person must be a U.S. citizen, U.S. national, U.S. resident alien, or a resident of Canada or Mexico.
case_text: Case file 5832 contains the tax documents compiled for Sofia Petrova. The taxpayer explicitly designates the individual as a qualifying child on the filing, relying exclusively on that category. By relationship, the person is the taxpayer's son or daughter. A comparison of birth dates shows the taxpayer is older than the dependent by 3 years. Residence records demonstrate the dependent maintained a shared household with the taxpayer for a total of 7 months. Financial ledgers indicate that 100% of the dependent's overall financial maintenance was provided by the taxpayer. Enrollment documentation confirms the dependent maintained full-time student status during a span of 5 months within the calendar year. The dependent and their spouse submitted a joint tax return for the year 2026. Household notes remark that the individual frequently assists with domestic chores. Leisure activities for the individual involve participating in a regional weekend orchestra. Form 1099 records show the individual accrued $500 in taxable interest. The case file contains no executed Form 2120 agreements from any secondary contributors. At the close of the tax year, the taxpayer had reached the age of 26. Weekly schedules for the household typically include attending services at the neighborhood house of worship. Gross rental payments collected by the individual amounted to $1,200 prior to accounting for maintenance expenses. Logistical logs establish that the dependent resided elsewhere during the remaining months under permanent, non-temporary arrangements. The joint filing was submitted to address overall tax liability rather than merely claiming a refund of excess withholdings. The taxpayer is not claimed as a dependent on any other individual's tax filing. Verification checks verify that no other filer lists this individual as a qualifying child. Independent financial calculations show the individual funded 20% of their living expenses using personal earnings.

policy_text:
Claiming a dependent on a 2026 federal return: qualifying child and qualifying relative tests
A taxpayer may claim the person as a dependent only if every rule below is met. Rules about a qualifying child apply only when the person is claimed as a qualifying child, and rules about a qualifying relative only when claimed as a qualifying relative. Rules marked as defaults say what to assume when the return is silent on a point.

R1. A qualifying child must have lived with the taxpayer for more than half the year (7 months or more). This rule does not apply if the time away was a temporary absence, such as for school, illness or military service.
R2. The taxpayer must provide more than half of a qualifying relative's total support.
R3. The person must be a U.S. citizen, U.S. national, U.S. resident alien, or a resident of Canada or Mexico.
R4. A qualifying child may not have paid for more than half of their own support.
R5. A qualifying child must be younger than the taxpayer, unless permanently and totally disabled.
R6. The person may not file a joint return for the year.
R7. If the return does not describe the time away as a temporary absence, count it as time not lived with the taxpayer.
R8. A qualifying child must be under age 19 at the end of the year, unless the person was a full-time student for at least 5 months of the year and is under 24.
R9. A taxpayer who can be claimed as someone else's dependent may not claim any dependent.

Salary and wage earnings for the individual amounted to $9,000. Throughout 2026, the individual resided in the filer's dwelling for a total of 0 months. Financial institutions distributed $500 in taxable interest to the individual. The entirety of the individual's financial support, equating to 100%, was supplied by the filer. Another family member, with whom the individual resides for the majority of the year, also counts the individual as a qualifying child. The tax professional remarks that the paperwork is being submitted ahead of schedule to expedite the disbursement. Rules about a qualifying child apply only when the person is claimed as a qualifying child, and rules about a qualifying relative only when claimed as a qualifying relative. Rules marked as defaults say what to assume when the return is silent on a point.

R1. A qualifying child must have lived with the taxpayer for more than half the year (7 months or more).
R2. The person must be a U.S. citizen, U.S. national, U.S. resident alien, or a resident of Canada or Mexico, unless the taxpayer is a U.S. citizen who legally adopted the person and the person lived with the taxpayer all year.
R3. A qualifying child must be younger than the taxpayer, unless permanently and totally disabled.
R4. The taxpayer must provide more than half of a qualifying relative's total support.
R5. If a parent of the person also claims them as a qualifying child, a taxpayer who is not the person's parent may not claim them.
R6. If disability is not mentioned, assume the person is not permanently and totally disabled.
R7. The person may not file a joint return for the year.
R8. A qualifying relative who is not a listed relative (a cousin is not listed, but in-laws, parents, siblings, nieces and nephews are) must have lived with the taxpayer all year.
R9. A qualifying child must be under age 19 at the end of the year. This rule does not apply if the person was a full-time student for at least 5 months of the year and is under 24.

Rules about a qualifying child apply only when the person is claimed as a qualifying child, and rules about a qualifying relative only when claimed as a qualifying relative. Rules marked as defaults say what to assume when the return is silent on a point.

R1. A qualifying child must be the taxpayer's child, stepchild, placed foster child, brother or sister, or a descendant of one of them (such as a grandchild, niece or nephew).
R2. A qualifying child must be under age 19 at the end of the year. This rule does not apply if the person was a full-time student for at least 5 months of the year and is under 24.
R3. If disability is not mentioned, assume the person is not permanently and totally disabled.
R4. If the return does not say the person is another taxpayer's qualifying child, assume they are not.
R5. The taxpayer must provide more than half of a qualifying relative's total support.
R6. A qualifying child must have lived with the taxpayer for more than half the year (7 months or more). This rule does not apply if the time away was a temporary absence, such as for school, illness or military service.
R7. The person must be a U.S. citizen, U.S. national, U.S. resident alien, or a resident of Canada or Mexico.
R8. A qualifying relative who is not a listed relative (a cousin is not listed, but in-laws, parents, siblings, nieces and nephews are) must have lived with the taxpayer all year.
R9. A qualifying child must be younger than the taxpayer, unless permanently and totally disabled.
R10. A qualifying relative may not be the qualifying child of any other taxpayer.

policy_text:
Claiming a dependent on a 2026 federal return: qualifying child and qualifying relative tests
A taxpayer may claim the person as a dependent only if every rule below is met. Rules about a qualifying child apply only when the person is claimed as a qualifying child, and rules about a qualifying relative only when claimed as a qualifying relative. Rules marked as defaults say what to assume when the return is silent on a point.

R1. A taxpayer who can be claimed as someone else's dependent may not claim any dependent.
R2. The person must be a U.S. citizen, U.S. national, U.S. resident alien, or a resident of Canada or Mexico.
R3. A qualifying child must be under age 19 at the end of the year. This rule does not apply if the person was a full-time student for at least 5 months of the year and is under 24.
R4. If the return does not say someone else can claim the taxpayer, assume no one can.
R5. A qualifying child must be younger than the taxpayer, unless permanently and totally disabled.
R6. The taxpayer must provide more than half of a qualifying relative's total support. This rule does not apply if a signed multiple support agreement (Form 2120) names the taxpayer, who provides more than 10% of the support.
R7. A qualifying child may not have paid for more than half of their own support.
R8. A qualifying relative may not be the qualifying child of any other taxpayer.

R8. A qualifying child must be under age 19 at the end of the year.
R9. If a joint return is not described as filed only for a refund, assume it is not.

Rules about a qualifying child apply only when the person is claimed as a qualifying child, and rules about a qualifying relative only when claimed as a qualifying relative. Rules marked as defaults say what to assume when the return is silent on a point.

R1. A qualifying child must have lived with the taxpayer for more than half the year (7 months or more), unless the time away was a temporary absence, such as for school, illness or military service.
R2. The taxpayer must provide more than half of a qualifying relative's total support, unless a signed multiple support agreement (Form 2120) names the taxpayer, who provides more than 10% of the support.
R3. If disability is not mentioned, assume the person is not permanently and totally disabled.
R4. A qualifying child must be younger than the taxpayer, unless permanently and totally disabled.
R5. A qualifying child must be under age 19 at the end of the year. This rule does not apply if the person was a full-time student for at least 5 months of the year and is under 24.
R6. A qualifying relative who is not a listed relative (a cousin is not listed, but in-laws, parents, siblings, nieces and nephews are) must have lived with the taxpayer all year.
R7. A qualifying child must be the taxpayer's child, stepchild, placed foster child, brother or sister, or a descendant of one of them (such as a grandchild, niece or nephew).
R8. The person must be a U.S. citizen, U.S. national, U.S. resident alien, or a resident of Canada or Mexico. This rule does not apply if the taxpayer is a U.S. citizen who legally adopted the person and the person lived with the taxpayer all year.

The taxpayer's own mother and father are eligible to claim the taxpayer as a dependent on their tax filing. The time spent away from the residence constituted a temporary absence for educational purposes, and the individual's personal bedroom remained reserved for them. Financial institutions distributed $500 in taxable interest income to the individual. The parent with primary custody has not executed a release of the dependency claim using Form 8332. The individual provided 60% of their total financial maintenance throughout the calendar year. The joint tax return requests specific credits rather than solely seeking a refund of tax withheld. The individual resided at the taxpayer's primary dwelling for the entire 12 months of 2026. The tax professional noted in the margins that the documents are being submitted ahead of schedule to expedite the client's refund. A separate taxpayer lists the individual as a qualifying child. Half of all funds utilized to support the individual were contributed directly by the taxpayer. The individual maintains their permanent residence in India and does not hold U.S. citizenship, national status, or residency. The individual is submitting an individual tax return and is not filing jointly with a spouse. When combining wages, taxable interest, and rental receipts prior to any deductions, the individual's total gross income reaches $5,700. The taxpayer, who holds U.S. citizenship, completed a legal adoption of the individual. Within the tax forms, the individual is designated exclusively as a qualifying child, relying solely on that specific criterion. None of the auxiliary contributors executed a Form 2120 multiple support declaration. The taxpayer reached the age of 20 by the conclusion of the tax year. During the weekends, the individual participates in a local community orchestra. The taxpayer inquired whether the paperwork could be transmitted to the agency through electronic filing systems. Following an unforeseen accident, the individual has suffered from a permanent and total disability. The family connection between the parties is that the individual is the son or daughter of the taxpayer. The individual was enrolled as a full-time student spanning a period of at least 5 months during the year. The individual collected $1,200 in rental payments from an occupant before subtracting any operating expenses. Neither of the individual's biological parents is attempting to claim them on a tax return.

A taxpayer may claim the person as a dependent only if every rule below is met. Rules about a qualifying child apply only when the person is claimed as a qualifying child, and rules about a qualifying relative only when claimed as a qualifying relative. Rules marked as defaults say what to assume when the return is silent on a point.

R8. A qualifying child must be under age 19 at the end of the year. This rule does not apply if the person was a full-time student for at least 5 months of the year and is under 24.
R9. A qualifying relative who is not a listed relative (a cousin is not listed, but in-laws, parents, siblings, nieces and nephews are) must have lived with the taxpayer all year.

policy_text:
Claiming a dependent on a 2026 federal return: qualifying child and qualifying relative tests
A taxpayer may claim the person as a dependent only if every rule below is met. Rules about a qualifying child apply only when the person is claimed as a qualifying child, and rules about a qualifying relative only when claimed as a qualifying relative. Rules marked as defaults say what to assume when the return is silent on a point.

R1. The taxpayer must provide more than half of a qualifying relative's total support, unless a signed multiple support agreement (Form 2120) names the taxpayer, who provides more than 10% of the support.
R2. A taxpayer who can be claimed as someone else's dependent may not claim any dependent.
R3. A qualifying relative's gross income, which counts wages, taxable interest and rent received before expenses, must be less than $5,300.
R4. A qualifying child may not have paid for more than half of their own support.
R5. A qualifying child must be under age 19 at the end of the year. This rule does not apply if the person was a full-time student for at least 5 months of the year and is under 24.
R6. If no multiple support agreement is mentioned, assume there is none.
R7. The person must be a U.S. citizen, U.S. national, U.S. resident alien, or a resident of Canada or Mexico.
R8. If the return does not say someone else can claim the taxpayer, assume no one can.

policy_text:
Claiming a dependent on a 2026 federal return: qualifying child and qualifying relative tests
A taxpayer may claim the person as a dependent only if every rule below is met. Rules about a qualifying child apply only when the person is claimed as a qualifying child, and rules about a qualifying relative only when claimed as a qualifying relative. Rules marked as defaults say what to assume when the return is silent on a point.

R1. A qualifying child must have lived with the taxpayer for more than half the year (7 months or more). This rule does not apply if the time away was a temporary absence, such as for school, illness or military service.
R2. A qualifying child may not have paid for more than half of their own support.
R3. A qualifying child must be under age 19 at the end of the year, unless the person was a full-time student for at least 5 months of the year and is under 24.
R4. If no parent is said to claim the person, assume no parent does.
R5. A qualifying relative who is not a listed relative (a cousin is not listed, but in-laws, parents, siblings, nieces and nephews are) must have lived with the taxpayer all year.
R6. The person must be a U.S. citizen, U.S. national, U.S. resident alien, or a resident of Canada or Mexico.
R7. A qualifying child must be younger than the taxpayer, unless permanently and totally disabled.
R8. A qualifying child must be the taxpayer's child, stepchild, placed foster child, brother or sister, or a descendant of one of them (such as a grandchild, niece or nephew).
R9. If a parent of the person also claims them as a qualifying child, a taxpayer who is not the person's parent may not claim them.
R10. The taxpayer must provide more than half of a qualifying relative's total support.
